claim: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are a class of small regulatory non-coding RNAs that participate in various biological functions by repressing gene expression post-transcriptionally.
source: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are a class of small regulatory non-coding RNAs that participate in various biological functions by repressing gene expression post-transcriptionally (Ambros, 2004; Bartel, 2004; He and Hannon, 2004; Kim, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature (Ambros, 2004; Bartel, 2004; He and Hannon, 2004; Kim, 2005).

claim: Global depletion of miRNAs through Dicer knockout leads to obvious defects in embryonic development, from cell differentiation to animal survival.
source: Several mouse knockout (KO) studies of Dicer, the pivotal RNase for generating mature miRNAs, have revealed that global depletion of these small regulatory RNAs leads to obvious defects in embryonic development, from cell differentiation to animal survival, underlining the functional importance of miRNAs during embryonic development (Bernstein et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2011; Harfe et al., 2005; Kanellopoulou et al., 2005; Tung et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to mouse knockout studies (Bernstein et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2011; Harfe et al., 2005; Kanellopoulou et al., 2005; Tung et al., 2015).

claim: Loss-of-function studies on most individual miRNAs have revealed minor or no overt developmental or behavioral phenotypes in multiple organisms.
source: However, loss-of-function studies on most individual miRNAs have revealed minor or no overt developmental or behavioral phenotypes in multiple organisms, partly reflecting the functional redundancy of miRNAs due to their polycistronic and paralogous features (Alvarez-Saavedra and Horvitz, 2010; Miska et al., 2007; Olive et al., 2015; Park et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies across organisms (Alvarez-Saavedra and Horvitz, 2010; Miska et al., 2007; Olive et al., 2015; Park et al., 2012).

claim: A single miRNA can target multiple mRNAs, and a targeted mRNA can also be bound by different miRNAs at its 3ʹ untranslated region (3ʹ UTR) with differential stoichiometric affinities.
source: Moreover, a single miRNA can target multiple mRNAs, and a targeted mRNA can also be bound by different miRNAs at its 3ʹ untranslated region (3ʹ UTR) with differential stoichiometric affinities, representing a reciprocal one-to-multiple regulatory mechanism (Bartel, 2009; Krek et al., 2005; Loh et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on miRNA-mRNA interactions (Bartel, 2009; Krek et al., 2005; Loh et al., 2011).

claim: The MiR34/449 family comprises six homologous miRNAs (MiR34a, 34b, 34c, 449a, 449b, and 449c) located at three different genomic loci.
source: One well-characterized example of a polycistronic miRNA family is MiR34/449, which comprises six homologous miRNAs (MiR34a, 34b, 34c, 449a, 449b, and 449c) located at three different genomic loci—Mir34a, Mir34b/c, and Mir449a/b/c (Mir449)—that encode evolutionary-conserved sequences among vertebrates (Olive et al., 2015; Song et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies characterizing the MiR34/449 family (Olive et al., 2015; Song et al., 2014).

claim: MiR34a, MiR34b, and MiR34c appear to be direct targets of p53 and have been shown to be involved in p53-mediated apoptosis in cancer contexts.
source: The MiR34a, MiR34b, and MiR34c (MiR34) miRNAs appear to be direct targets of p53, and they have been shown to be involved in p53-mediated apoptosis in cancer contexts (Bommer et al., 2007; Corney et al., 2007; He et al., 2007; Raver-Shapira et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on p53-mediated regulation of MiR34 (Bommer et al., 2007; Corney et al., 2007; He et al., 2007; Raver-Shapira et al., 2007).

claim: The Mir449 cluster is embedded in the second intron of a host gene, Cdc20b.
source: Whereas Mir34a and Mir34bc are not located within other genes, the Mir449 cluster is embedded in the second intron of a host gene, Cdc20b (cell division cycle 20 homologue B), and similar expression patterns of MiR449 and Cdc20b in mouse testis support that they may be subjected to the same mechanism of transcriptional regulation (Bao et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on the genomic location of Mir449 (Bao et al., 2012).

claim: MiR449 has a role in regulating multiciliogenesis by suppressing the Notch pathway.
source: Apart from this functional redundancy in the context of DNA damage, an additional role for MiR449 in regulating multiciliogenesis by suppressing the Notch pathway has been demonstrated (Lizé et al., 2011; Marcet et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating MiR449's role in multiciliogenesis (Lizé et al., 2011; Marcet et al., 2011).

claim: Mature MiR34a is ubiquitously expressed in a variety of organs, whereas MiR34bc and MiR449 exhibit a cell-type-specific expression pattern.
source: Mature MiR34a has been shown to be ubiquitously expressed in a variety of organs, whereas MiR34bc and MiR449 exhibit a cell-type-specific expression pattern, predominantly in ciliated cells, such as in respiratory and reproductive tissues, as well as in the ependymal cells enriched with cilia responsible for cerebrospinal fluid flow within the CNS (Bao et al., 2012; Kasai et al., 2016; Olive et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on MiR34/449 expression patterns (Bao et al., 2012; Kasai et al., 2016; Olive et al., 2015).

claim: MiR34/449 displays compensatory expression upon single KO in a context-dependent manner.
source: Due to their shared and redundant seed sequences, MiR34/449 displays compensatory expression upon single KO in a context-dependent manner, emphasizing the necessity to enact combinatorial KO of all Mir34/449 alleles (Bao et al., 2012; Choi et al., 2017; Concepcion et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating compensatory expression (Bao et al., 2012; Choi et al., 2017; Concepcion et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2014).

claim: The most prominent phenotype arising from MiR34/449 ablation is the impairment of motile ciliogenesis, which results in respiratory dysfunction, male/female infertility, and postnatal lethality.
source: Based on three studies of Mir34bc and Mir449 double KO (DKO) mice, as well as Mir34/449 triple KO (TKO) mice, the most prominent phenotype arising from MiR34/449 ablation is the impairment of motile ciliogenesis, which results in respiratory dysfunction, male/female infertility, and postnatal lethality (Otto et al., 2017; Song et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2014; Yuan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on MiR34/449 knockout phenotypes (Otto et al., 2017; Song et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2014; Yuan et al., 2019).

claim: MiR34/449 exhibits a dynamic expression pattern during spinal cord development.
source: We previously uncovered that MiR34/449 exhibits a dynamic expression pattern during spinal cord development (Li et al., 2017), so we hypothesized that MiR34/449 might exert an as yet uncharacterized function in the spinal cord.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors (Li et al., 2017).

claim: The spinal cord is one of the most important executive centers for body movement, conveying somatosensory information and integrating motor commands.
source: The spinal cord is one of the most important executive centers for body movement, conveying somatosensory information and integrating motor commands emanating from spinal cord per se or the brain (Arber, 2017; Arber and Costa, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on spinal cord function (Arber, 2017; Arber and Costa, 2018).

claim: Interneurons in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord terminate in exteroceptive sensory fibers and mediate sensory processing.
source: Interneurons (INs) that reside in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord terminate in exteroceptive sensory fibers and mediate sensory processing.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of spinal cord anatomy and function.

claim: The ventral horn contains both motor neurons (MNs) and various INs, which are critical for motor function and for generating the rhythmicity of motor behaviors.
source: The ventral horn contains both motor neurons (MNs) and various INs, which are critical for motor function and for generating the rhythmicity of motor behaviors (Dasen, 2018; Garcia-Campmany et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on ventral horn function (Dasen, 2018; Garcia-Campmany et al., 2010).

claim: The intermediate region of the dorso-ventral spinal cord serves as a relay station that receives multiple convergent inputs from proprioceptive, exteroceptive, and corticospinal neurons.
source: This region serves as a relay station that receives multiple convergent inputs from proprioceptive, exteroceptive, and corticospinal neurons, which connect monosynaptically to MNs (Levine et al., 2014; Tripodi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on intermediate spinal cord function (Levine et al., 2014; Tripodi et al., 2011).

claim: Activation of premotor neurons (motor synergy encoders, MSE) induces multiple motor pools that contribute to complex movements.
source: Activation of these premotor neurons, denoted motor synergy encoders (MSE), induces multiple motor pools that contribute to complex movements (Levine et al., 2014; Osseward and Pfaff, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on MSE neurons (Levine et al., 2014; Osseward and Pfaff, 2019).

claim: Conditional ablation of Satb2 from the intermediate spinal cord results in a hyperflexion phenotype upon triggering the limb withdrawal reflex.
source: Conditional ablation of Satb2 from the intermediate spinal cord results in a hyperflexion phenotype upon triggering the limb withdrawal reflex (Hilde et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on Satb2 function (Hilde et al., 2016).

claim: miRNAs are critical regulators during embryonic spinal cord development, playing roles in progenitor patterning, subtype specification, functional maintenance, and neural regeneration.
source: It is well documented that miRNAs are critical regulators during embryonic spinal cord development, playing roles in progenitor patterning, subtype specification, functional maintenance, and neural regeneration (Chen et al., 2011; Chen and Wichterle, 2012; Chen and Chen, 2019; Kye and Gonçalves, 2014; Tung et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on miRNA function in spinal cord development (Chen et al., 2011; Chen and Wichterle, 2012; Chen and Chen, 2019; Kye and Gonçalves, 2014; Tung et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2013).

claim: Loss of Dicer from late-stage post-mitotic spinal MNs using ChAT-Cre results in development of a spinal muscular atrophy (SMA)-like phenotype in a mouse model.
source: Notably, loss of Dicer from late-stage post-mitotic spinal MNs using ChAT-Cre results in development of a spinal muscular atrophy (SMA)-like phenotype in a mouse model (Haramati et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on Dicer knockout in motor neurons (Haramati et al., 2010).

claim: Mice in which Dicer has been knocked out from proprioceptive sensory neurons display impaired maintenance of monosynaptic sensory-motor circuits in the spinal cord.
source: Furthermore, mice in which Dicer has been knocked out from proprioceptive sensory neurons display impaired maintenance of monosynaptic sensory-motor circuits in the spinal cord (Imai et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on Dicer knockout in sensory neurons (Imai et al., 2016).

claim: MiR34a-5p is expressed in most spinal cord neurons, including ventral MNs and most dorsal INs.
source: For both embryonic and postnatal stages, we found that MiR34a-5p is expressed in most spinal cord neurons (Figure 1M), including ventral MNs (Figure 1N) and most dorsal INs (Figure 1O).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 1M, 1N, and 1O.

claim: MiR34a-5p exhibits the strongest expression in the spinal cord among MiR34/449 members, with low embryonic-stage expression and increasing levels as postnatal stages progress.
source: Among the MiR34/449 members, MiR34a-5p exhibits the strongest expression in the spinal cord, with low embryonic-stage expression and increasing levels as postnatal stages progress.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in the manuscript showing temporal expression patterns.

claim: Both Mir34bc/449 DKO and Mir34/449 TKO mice exhibit partial postnatal lethality and growth retardation with reduced body weight.
source: Consistent with previously reported phenotypes for these lines, both Mir34/449 TKO and Mir34bc/449 DKO mice exhibited partial postnatal lethality and growth retardation with reduced body weight (Figure 2B and C; Fededa et al., 2016; Song et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2B and 2C, as well as citations to previous studies (Fededa et al., 2016; Song et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2014).

claim: Both Mir34bc/449 DKO and Mir34/449 TKO mice presented two waves of postnatal mortality: a first wave occurred after the first week (P7~P14), with a second wave between P21 and P28.
source: Unexpectedly, both the Mir34bc/449 DKO and Mir34/449 TKO mice presented two waves of postnatal mortality: a first wave occurred after the first week (P7~P14) (Song et al., 2014), with a second wave between P21 and P28 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2B and a citation to a previous study (Song et al., 2014).

claim: Approximately 50% of Mir34bc/449 DKO and Mir34/449 TKO mice died within the first 2 weeks of birth, with an additional ~40% died within 4 weeks.
source: Approximately 50% of Mir34bc/449 DKO and Mir34/449 TKO mice died within the first 2 weeks of birth, with an additional ~40% died within 4 weeks (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Only ~10% of Mir34bc/449 DKO and Mir34/449 TKO mice survived to adulthood with less obvious growth retardation or abnormalities.
source: Consequently, only ~10% of mice survived to adulthood with less obvious growth retardation or abnormalities.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the survival data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mir34bc/449 DKO and Mir34/449 TKO mice manifested several unusual abnormalities, including blepharoptosis, abnormal posture (back-arching), and uncoordinated hind tiptoe walking and jumpy behavior.
source: For instance, we found that Mir34bc/449 DKO and Mir34/449 TKO mice presented significantly reduced body weights relative to respective controls (Figure 2C), and they manifested several unusual abnormalities, including blepharoptosis (ptosis, drooping eyelids) or microphthalmia (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), abnormal posture (back-arching; Figure 2D), and uncoordinated hind tiptoe walking and jumpy behavior, which resemble neurological deficits related to sensory-motor function defects (Imai et al., 2016; Figure 2—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 2C, 2D, and supplementary figures, as well as videos.

claim: MN differentiation is not affected by Mir34/449 locus deletion.
source: Next, we investigated if MN differentiation was abrogated by Mir34/449 locus deletion. We crossed our Mir34/449 TKO mice with the MN reporter Hb9::GFP mouse line to facilitate MN identification. The number and distribution of post-mitotic MNs were comparable between MiR34/449-deficient and Ctrl embryos (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MN subtype identity is not altered in MiR34/449-deficient embryos at E12.5.
source: However, MN subtype identity did not appear to be altered in MiR34/449-deficient embryos at E12.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: MiR34/449 miRNAs do not play an overt role in MN development.
source: Thus, MiR34/449 miRNAs do not play an overt role in MN development.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of observed differences in MN development in MiR34/449-deficient mice.

claim: Both Mir34bc/449 DKO and Mir34/449 TKO mice exhibited slightly yet significantly reduced locomotor activity relative to WT and Ctrl mice.
source: Our results show that both Mir34bc/449 DKO and Mir34/449 TKO mice exhibited slightly yet significantly reduced locomotor activity relative to WT and Ctrl mice (Figure 3B), while their locomotor coordination appeared normal assayed by the rotarod (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by open field test data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Locomotor coordination of Mir34bc/449 DKO and Mir34/449 TKO mice appeared normal as assayed by the rotarod.
source: Our results show that both Mir34bc/449 DKO and Mir34/449 TKO mice exhibited slightly yet significantly reduced locomotor activity relative to WT and Ctrl mice (Figure 3B), while their locomotor coordination appeared normal assayed by the rotarod (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by rotarod test data shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: Obvious and spontaneous jumpy movements were recorded in the home cages of Mir34bc/449 DKO and Mir34/449 TKO mice, as well as in the open arena (occurrence ~35%).
source: Notably, we recorded obvious and spontaneous jumpy movements in the home cages of Mir34bc/449 DKO and Mir34/449 TKO mice, as well as in the open arena (occurrence ~35%; Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral observations documented in videos.

claim: The overall motor function appeared hyper-jumpy while most motor outputs were largely preserved upon loss of MiR34/449 miRNAs.
source: Based on these findings, we suggest that the overall motor function appeared hyper-jumpy while most motor outputs were largely preserved upon loss of MiR34/449 miRNAs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the behavioral assay results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The response threshold in nociceptive withdrawal behavior to mechanical stimulation was comparable among WT, Ctrl, and MiR34/449 mutant lines.
source: We first performed a von Frey test on MiR34/449 mutants, Ctrl and WT mice to measure their responses to mechanical stimulation, and observed that the response threshold in nociceptive withdrawal behavior was comparable among WT, Ctrl, and MiR34/449 mutant lines (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by von Frey test data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: MiR34/449 mutant mice displayed a significantly reduced latency in the tail flick test relative to both Ctrl and WT mice.
source: We found that MiR34/449 mutant mice displayed a significantly reduced latency in the tail flick test relative to both Ctrl and WT mice (Figure 4C), indicative of increased sensitivity to heat stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by tail flick test data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: MiR34/449 mutant mice exhibited increased sensitivity to heat stimulation.
source: We found that MiR34/449 mutant mice displayed a significantly reduced latency in the tail flick test relative to both Ctrl and WT mice (Figure 4C), indicative of increased sensitivity to heat stimulation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the reduced latency in the tail flick test.

claim: A minor (but not statistically significant) decrease in hindlimb response latency was observed among MiR34/449 mutant mice in the hot-plate experiment when compared to WT and Ctrl mice.
source: We then performed a hot-plate experiment whereby a heat stimulus is applied to the hind paws of mice, as this assay is considered to involve more complex supraspinal pathways (Giglio et al., 2006). We observed a minor (but not statistically significant) decrease in hindlimb response latency among MiR34/449 mutant mice when compared to WT and Ctrl mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by hot-plate test data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The major function of MiR34/449 in the spinal cord relates to spinal reflex circuits.
source: Thus, we suggest that the major function of MiR34/449 in the spinal cord relates to spinal reflex circuits.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects observed in tail flick (spinal reflex) versus hot-plate (supraspinal) tests.

claim: Satb1 and Satb2 are potential candidate targets of MiR34/449 that are predicted to participate in IN specification or maturation.
source: Based on those criteria, we identified potential candidate targets of MiR34/449 that were predicted to participate in IN specification or maturation, including multiple genes previously characterized as being important in INs, that is, Satb1, Satb2 (Figure 5B and Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic predictions and filtering criteria described in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Co-transfection of the luciferase construct with three MiR34/449 expression vectors resulted in a reduction in luciferase activity for the WT 3ʹ UTRs of Satb1/2 constructs.
source: Co-transfection of the luciferase construct with three MiR34/449 expression vectors resulted in a reduction in luciferase activity for the WT 3ʹ UTRs of Satb1/2 constructs (Figure 5C and D), whereas a construct harboring the mutated targeting sequences was completely insensitive to miRNA-mediated silencing (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: A construct harboring the mutated targeting sequences was completely insensitive to miRNA-mediated silencing.
source: Co-transfection of the luciferase construct with three MiR34/449 expression vectors resulted in a reduction in luciferase activity for the WT 3ʹ UTRs of Satb1/2 constructs (Figure 5C and D), whereas a construct harboring the mutated targeting sequences was completely insensitive to miRNA-mediated silencing (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: MiR34/449 targets the 3ʹ UTRs of Satb1 and Satb2.
source: These findings indicate that MiR34/449 targets the 3ʹ UTRs of Satb1 and Satb2.
evidence: This claim is supported by the luciferase assay results demonstrating direct targeting.

claim: A significantly increased number of Satb1on and Satb2on INs was observed in the MiR34/449 mutant spinal cords at P14 compared to WT and control littermates.
source: Notably, a previous study characterized the cellular identity of MSE neurons and found that Satb1/2 are expressed in medial lamina V/VI and lamina III (Levine et al., 2014). Unlike for WT and control littermates at P14, we observed a significantly increased number of Satb1on and Satb2on INs in the MiR34/449 mutant spinal cords (Figure 5E~5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 5E-5G.

claim: A drastic increase in the number of hybrid cells expressing both Satb1 and Satb2 was observed in the MiR34/449 mutant spinal cords at P14 compared to WT and Ctrl groups.
source: Moreover, we also observed a drastic increase in the number of hybrid cells expressing both Satb1 and Satb2 in the MiR34/449 mutant spinal cords at P14 compared to WT and Ctrl groups (Figure 5E and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 5E and 5H.

claim: Satb1 and Satb2 are directly regulated by MiR34/449 miRNAs in the spinal cord.
source: Thus, we have shown that Satb1 and Satb2 are directly regulated by MiR34/449 miRNAs in the spinal cord.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combination of luciferase assays and in vivo expression data.

claim: Many Satb1/2on INs co-expressed MiR34a-5p or MiR34c-5p in the dorsal/intermediate regions of the spinal cord at P14.
source: Notably, we identified many Satb1/2on INs that co-expressed MiR34a-5p or MiR34c-5p in the dorsal/intermediate regions of the spinal cord at P14, suggesting potentially direct regulation of Satb1/2 by MiR34/449 in spinal INs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: MiR34/449 may control optimal development of Satb1/2on INs in the spinal cord to fine-tune sensory-motor circuit outputs.
source: Together, these findings indicate that MiR34/449 may control optimal development of Satb1/2on INs in the spinal cord to fine-tune sensory-motor circuit outputs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined results of targeting experiments and behavioral phenotypes.

claim: There were no apparent differences in IN progenitors in the dorsal or ventral horns at E11.5 in MiR34/449 mutant embryos.
source: At E11.5, there were no apparent differences in IN progenitors in the dorsal or ventral horns—as revealed by molecular markers Lbx1 (dI4 ~6), Lhx1/5 (dI2, 4, 6~V1), Isl1 (dI3), and Tlx3 (dI3, 5) for the dorsal horn, or Foxd3 (dI2, V1), Chx10 (V2a), and Lhx3 (V2) for the ventral horn, respectively—indicating that MiR34/449 is not required for most IN development (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A~K).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A-K.

claim: MiR34/449 is not required for most IN development.
source: At E11.5, there were no apparent differences in IN progenitors in the dorsal or ventral horns—as revealed by molecular markers Lbx1 (dI4 ~6), Lhx1/5 (dI2, 4, 6~V1), Isl1 (dI3), and Tlx3 (dI3, 5) for the dorsal horn, or Foxd3 (dI2, V1), Chx10 (V2a), and Lhx3 (V2) for the ventral horn, respectively—indicating that MiR34/449 is not required for most IN development (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A~K).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of observed differences in IN progenitors.

claim: At E13.5, there was no significant difference in numbers of Satb2on INs in MiR34/449 mutant spinal cords relative to WT and Ctrl.
source: At E13.5 (the earliest time-point at which we could detect dorsal Satb2 INs), there was no significant difference in numbers of Satb2on INs in MiR34/449 mutant spinal cords relative to WT and Ctrl (Figure 5—figure supplement 3L and M).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3L and M.

claim: There was a dramatic increase of Satb2on INs relative to WT and Ctrl at P14 in the MiR34/449 mutant spinal cords throughout the spinal cord segments.
source: Although comparable numbers of Satb2on INs persisted until E16.5 (data not shown), there was a dramatic increase of Satb2on INs relative to WT and Ctrl at P14 in the MiR34/449 mutant spinal cords throughout the spinal cord segments (Figure 5E and F and Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 5E, 5F, and Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Optimal Satb2on IN number and maintenance is particularly sensitive to MiR34/449 expression in the postnatal spinal cord.
source: This outcome indicates that optimal Satb2on IN number and maintenance is particularly sensitive to MiR34/449 expression in the postnatal spinal cord.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the temporal pattern of Satb2 expression changes.

claim: MiR34/449 miRNAs control optimal development of Satb2-expressing INs in the spinal cord, particularly at the postnatal stage.
source: Collectively, we suggest that MiR34/449 miRNAs control optimal development of Satb2-expressing INs in the spinal cord, particularly at the postnatal stage, enabling this miRNA family to fine-tune and maintain sensory-motor circuit outputs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined temporal and functional data.

claim: Neither Satb1 or Satb2 expressing IN positions were obviously affected in the absence of MiR34/449 at P14.
source: Given that the position of the Satb2on INs is highly associated with the connectivity of the sensory afferents (Hilde et al., 2016; Levine et al., 2014), we next tested if the position of the Satb1on or Satb2on INs is affected in the absence of the MiR34/449 at P14. However, neither Satb1 or Satb2 expressing IN positions were obviously affected (Figure 5—figure supplement 5), reflecting the different phenotype manifestation between MiR34/449 mutants and Satb2 KO mice (Hilde et al., 2016; Levine et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial distribution analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: An increase in the number of Satb2on;Ctip2on INs was observed in the MiR34/449 mutant spinal cords.
source: Notably, we observed an increase in the number of Satb2on;Ctip2on INs in the MiR34/449 mutant spinal cords (Figure 6A and B), yet only a subtle (but not statistically significant) change in the Satb2on;Pax2on IN subpopulation was found (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: Only a subtle (but not statistically significant) change in the Satb2on;Pax2on IN subpopulation was found in MiR34/449 mutant spinal cords.
source: Notably, we observed an increase in the number of Satb2on;Ctip2on INs in the MiR34/449 mutant spinal cords (Figure 6A and B), yet only a subtle (but not statistically significant) change in the Satb2on;Pax2on IN subpopulation was found (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 6A and 6C.

claim: The Satb2on;Ctip2on IN subpopulation had preferentially increased, with a concomitant decrease in the Satb2on;Pax2on subpopulation, in the Mir34/449 TKO spinal cords relative to those of WT and control littermates.
source: As the individual Ctip2on and Pax2on cell populations were of comparable size, this outcome further indicates that the Satb2on;Ctip2on IN subpopulation had preferentially increased, with a concomitant decrease in the Satb2on;Pax2on subpopulation, in the Mir34/449 TKO spinal cords relative to those of WT and control littermates (Figure 6D and G).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the quantification data shown in Figures 6D and 6G.

claim: The increased number of Satb2on;Ctip2on cells tended to exhibit a more condensed pattern in the intermediate region of the MiR34/449 mutant spinal cord.
source: Further spatial distribution analyses revealed no significant change in the distribution of the increased number of Satb2on;Ctip2on, yet these cells tended to exhibit a more condensed pattern in the intermediate region of the MiR34/449 mutant spinal cord (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial distribution analysis shown in Figures 6E and 6F.

claim: MiR34/449 controls optimal development of Satb2-expressing INs in the spinal cord, and loss of MiR34/449 leads to a change in the molecular identity of Satb2on IN subtypes.
source: Given all of these findings, we suggest that MiR34/449 controls optimal development of Satb2-expressing INs in the spinal cord, and that loss of MiR34/449 leads to a change in the molecular identity of Satb2on IN subtypes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data on Satb2 subpopulation changes.

claim: MiR34/449 has a potential role in maintaining precise cell identity in the postnatal spinal cord, which is critical for refining sensory-motor circuit outputs.
source: Our results reflect a potential role for these miRNAs in maintaining precise cell identity in the postnatal spinal cord, which is critical for refining sensory-motor circuit outputs (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined results and summarized in Figure 7.

claim: MiR34/449 depletion results in a change to a spinal IN population that might contribute to altered sensory-motor responses.
source: Our findings demonstrate that MiR34/449 depletion results in a change to a spinal IN population that might contribute to altered sensory-motor responses, thereby revealing an important role for MiR34/449 in regulating the sensory-motor circuitry.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined behavioral and molecular data.

claim: The loss of MiR34/449 miRNAs perturbs thermally induced pain response thresholds in mice.
source: Our behavioral assays reveal that the loss of MiR34/449 miRNAs perturb thermally induced pain response thresholds and compromised delicate motor output in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by the tail flick test data showing altered thermal sensitivity.

claim: The loss of MiR34/449 miRNAs compromised delicate motor output in mice.
source: Our behavioral assays reveal that the loss of MiR34/449 miRNAs perturb thermally induced pain response thresholds and compromised delicate motor output in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral assay data showing jumpy movements and altered locomotor activity.

claim: MiR34/449 directly target Satb1 and Satb2 to fine-tune the precise number of a sub-population of motor synergy encoder (MSE) neurons.
source: Mechanistically, MiR34/449 directly target Satb1 and Satb2 to fine-tune the precise number of a sub-population of motor synergy encoder (MSE) neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by the luciferase assays and the observed changes in Satb1/2 expressing neuron numbers.

claim: MiR34/449 fine-tunes optimal development of Satb1/2on interneurons in the spinal cord, thereby refining explicit sensory-to-motor circuit outputs.
source: Thus, MiR34/449 fine-tunes optimal development of Satb1/2on interneurons in the spinal cord, thereby refining explicit sensory-to-motor circuit outputs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined molecular and behavioral data.
